name: L-Cysteine
lead: Cysteine is a semiessential proteinogenic amino acid whose side chain carries a thiol (sulfhydryl) group. The L-form is a building block of proteins in all organisms; the thiol lets cysteine residues form disulfide bonds that stabilize protein structure, as in keratin, and bind metal ions [1]. Humans can usually make it from methionine through the transsulfuration pathway, and it is also supplied by foods such as poultry, eggs, beef and whole grains [1].

In appearance-related discussion, L-cysteine comes up as a precursor of glutathione, the cell's principal thiol antioxidant, because cysteine availability is proposed to influence which melanin type skin makes, and because cysteine-based keratin chemistry underlies hair structure and perms. It is sold as a supplement, appears in hair supplements, and has industrial uses in food processing and permanent-wave hair treatments [1][21][22]. Its acetylated derivative, N-acetylcysteine (NAC), is a long-established medicine used as a mucolytic and as an antidote to paracetamol poisoning, and has been explored in preliminary research on androgenetic alopecia [2][20].

No published human trial in the reference material tests supplemental L-cysteine itself for skin lightening or other cosmetic outcomes. Evidence for a pigment effect is indirect, drawn from biochemistry and from studies of related compounds.
infobox: Glutathione building block; keratin disulfide bonds [1][21]

paras: Cysteine has the formula HS-CH2-CH(NH2)-COOH. Its thiol is readily oxidized, and two cysteines linked by a disulfide bond form cystine [1]. The name derives from the Greek word for bladder, because it was first found in urinary stones [1].

In animals, synthesis starts from serine, with sulfur supplied by methionine via homocysteine; cystathionine beta-synthase and cystathionine gamma-lyase complete the pathway [1]. Cystathionine gamma-lyase deficiency lowers levels of cysteine, glutathione, taurine and hydrogen sulfide in cells [3].

Cysteine is the sulfur-containing precursor for glutathione. The Wikipedia article notes that orally supplied glutathione has negligible systemic availability, so the body must synthesize it from cysteine, glycine and glutamate, and that dietary cysteine and glycine can improve synthesis [1]. Cysteine also supplies sulfide for iron-sulfur clusters and is the source of endogenous hydrogen sulfide, a signalling molecule studied in the nervous and cardiovascular systems [1][4].

Glutathione is a tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine and glycine; Wikipedia identifies the first synthesis step, joining glutamate and cysteine, as rate-limiting, and notes that NAC, a cysteine prodrug, helps replenish intracellular glutathione [21]. In 1884 Eugen Baumann reduced cystine with zinc and named the product cysteine [1]. Industrially, most L-cysteine is made by hydrolysing animal material such as poultry feathers or hog hair; EU rules prohibit human hair as a source, and fermentation of engineered E. coli supplies synthetic material for kosher, halal and vegetarian needs [1].

In keratin, disulfide bonds between cysteine residues give hair its strength and shape. Wikipedia's hair-straightening article describes chemical straightening and Japanese thermal reconditioning as loosening these cysteine bonds before heat or neutralisation sets a new shape [22].

Skin-tone discussions mention cysteine because the pigment pathway makes yellow-to-red pheomelanin when dopaquinone reacts with cysteine, and Wikipedia describes pheomelanin production as highly dependent on cysteine availability [23]. The same article reports that human epidermis contains roughly 74% eumelanin and 26% pheomelanin largely irrespective of skin tone, with tone differences mainly reflecting total melanin amount [23]. Glutathione is likewise discussed in lightening contexts; oral glutathione itself has poor systemic availability, so proponents point to cysteine or NAC as precursors [21]. Whether oral cysteine changes skin tone in people has not been tested in the studies cited here.

In hair care, cysteine is used in permanent-wave products, chiefly in Asia, where it breaks disulfide bonds in keratin [1][22]. Some forum posters recommend cysteine-containing supplements for hair growth [5]. NAC has been under preliminary research for male pattern baldness, alone or with minoxidil, and is not an established treatment [20].

L-Cysteine is a processing aid in baking and a precursor for savoury flavors made through Maillard reactions [1]. It is mostly produced by hydrolysis of animal material such as poultry feathers or hog hair, with synthetic and fermentation routes available for kosher, halal or vegetarian use [1].

NAC is used as a mucolytic and for acetaminophen poisoning, where it restores depleted liver glutathione, and has been studied for respiratory disease and neuropsychiatric conditions [2][6]. A US drug label for an oral L-cysteine homeopathic product lists traditional symptom-relief statements and notes that homeopathic statements are not FDA-evaluated [7].

NAC was patented in 1960, entered medical use in 1968, and works in paracetamol overdose by replenishing glutathione that neutralises the toxic metabolite NAPQI; an intravenous US product (Acetadote) was approved in 2004 [20]. In 2021 Amazon removed NAC products from US sale after the FDA indicated NAC is a drug rather than a supplement, the FDA issued draft enforcement guidance in April 2022, and Amazon re-listed them in August 2022 [20][19].

Wikipedia reports that cysteine has been proposed to counter acetaldehyde toxicity: in a rat study 80% of animals given cysteine survived a lethal acetaldehyde dose versus 10% of controls, and a 2020 article suggested it may help hangover symptoms in humans [1]. Hacker News threads discussed a cysteine-containing vitamin supplement and hangovers in 2020 and 2026 [24][25].

No studies found on L-cysteine as a skin-lightening or other appearance agent. Human research on cysteine and NAC concerns medical conditions, including a randomized trial of NAC in Parkinson's disease [8], an NAC trial in sudden deafness [9], a phase 3 study of L-cysteine in erythropoietic protoporphyria [10], and small phase 1 and 2 registrations of L-cysteine in healthy lactating women, peritoneal dialysis patients, and atrophic gastritis [11][12][13]. Reviews describe antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity of NAC in respiratory disease [6].

Cysteine from food is part of normal protein intake. Supplement and label information sources advise asking a healthcare professional before use during pregnancy or breastfeeding [7]. A case report describes a fixed drug eruption caused by S-carboxymethyl-L-cysteine, a related mucolytic [14]. Detailed adverse-event rates for supplemental L-cysteine are not covered by the studies cited here.

Wikipedia states that cysteine is much more toxic than most other amino acids [1]. For NAC, reported adverse effects include nausea, vomiting and rash orally, and anaphylaxis-like reactions in about 3 to 6 percent of patients receiving it intravenously; it may interact with nitroglycerin [20].

On T Nation, L-cysteine is mentioned in several contexts: as a supplement some members used for low SHBG while on anabolic steroids [15][16], as part of a stack for irritability and sleep [17], in hair-growth advice [5], and as a glutathione and liver-support precursor via NAC [18]. A 2021 thread discussed a regulatory change affecting NAC supplements in the US [19].

Cysteine is an approved food additive (E920) used as a baking processing aid [1]. NAC's status as a supplement versus a drug was disputed in the US in 2021 to 2022, as reflected in a T Nation thread that year [19][20].

lore.intro: On forums, L-cysteine appears as a supplement-stack ingredient and as a glutathione precursor, usually mentioned in passing rather than as a primary appearance tool [15][17][18].

claims.believers: A T Nation post advises that L-cysteine helps hair growth and recommends a multi-ingredient hair product [5].
claims.experts: No published human trial in the sources tested supplemental L-cysteine for hair growth; its role in hair is described chiefly in keratin chemistry and in industrial perming [1].

claims.claim: Cysteine (or NAC) helps restore SHBG or hormone markers after steroid use
claims.believers: Posters recount being advised to take taurine, L-cysteine or NAC alongside tamoxifen to improve low SHBG after anabolic steroid cycles [15][16].
claims.experts: No trial in the reference material has examined cysteine for SHBG or hormone recovery.

claims.claim: Cysteine raises glutathione, so it protects the liver and body
claims.believers: Members note that NAC is a delivery form of cysteine and a precursor of glutathione, used to restore liver glutathione [18].
claims.experts: NAC is an established antidote for paracetamol poisoning because it restores hepatic glutathione [2]; broader benefits in healthy people are studied mainly in disease contexts [6].

claims.claim: Cysteine availability lightens skin by steering melanin toward pheomelanin
claims.believers: The idea circulates in skin-tone discussions alongside glutathione, as a precursor-based route to a lighter complexion.
claims.experts: No trials of oral L-cysteine for lightening were found among the sources; the pheomelanin shift is a proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: NAC or cysteine supplements grow hair
claims.believers: Forum posters recommend cysteine-containing hair products [5]; NAC is also discussed alongside minoxidil.
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes NAC for androgenetic alopecia as preliminary research and not an established treatment [20].

claims.believers: Posts and threads share a cysteine vitamin supplement said to ease hangover symptoms [24][25].
claims.experts: Wikipedia cites a 2020 article suggesting possible benefit and a rat study of acetaldehyde protection [1].
